title: Kubernetes Rolling Updates & Rollbacks | Zero Downtime Deployments Explained
description:
Learn how Kubernetes ensures zero downtime with Rolling Updates & Rollbacks!

In this step-by-step tutorial, I’ll show you how to safely update applications in production, monitor rollouts, and instantly rollback if something goes wrong. 

What you’ll learn in this video:
- What Rolling Updates & Rollbacks are in Kubernetes
- How Kubernetes ensures zero downtime with deployments
- Step-by-step demo of rolling updates using kubectl
- Rolling back to a stable version when things break
- How Kubernetes manages pods behind the scenes (maxUnavailable, maxSurge)
- Checking rollout history and deployment revisions
- When to use Rolling Updates vs Rollbacks in real-world CI/CD


▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ Timestamps  ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬

00:24 - Why Rolling Updates & Rollbacks matter in Kubernetes

04:51 - Handling a Buggy Application with Rollback 
07:11 - Tracking Rollout History in Kubernetes
07:36 - When to Use Rolling Updates vs Rollbacks
08:18 - Conclusion & Best Practices

transcript.text:
Hello everyone, welcome back to the channel. I am 
Nikhil Kumar. Today we are diving into something

super useful when managing live applications 
in Kubernetes. That is rolling updates and

roll backs. This is how Kubernetes helps you 
update applications with zero downtime. And yes,

if something goes wrong, you can quickly roll 
back to a previous version. Let's dive in. Imagine

you are updating your application in production. 
You don't want to take it down for users, right?

That's where rolling updates comes in. Kubernetes 
will gradually replace old pod with a new ones.

This ensures there's always a working version 
running and user will not face any disruption.

Kubernetes handles this with deployments where 
you define the image version you want to run,

the strategy for updates and by default Kubernetes 
uses a rolling update strategy. Now let's see it

in the action. So this is our Kubernetes cluster. 
So this is our two node cluster. First let's

create a deployment. I have already covered a 
deployment in very detail. I will add a link in

the description or the above I button so you can 
check it out as well. So to create a deployment

we can use a command kubectl create deployment 
rolling-demo and the image name that is equal

to nginx and the tag is 1.19. So deployment got 
created. Let's verify it very quickly. kubectl

get pods. We can see one pod is running with 
the rolling-demo. And if we see the deployment,

we can see the rolling-demo deployment is running. 
Now suppose we want to update the image to a new

version. Let's say we want to update the image 
to 1.21. As of now, it's 1.29. But in the new

version, we need to update it to 1.21. Let's 
try to do it very quickly. So for that we have

a command kubectl set image deployment and the 
deployment name that is rolling-demo and the

image. So for that we are going to use nginx 
equal to nginx 1.21. This triggers a rolling

update and you can also monitor it live. So 
for that we can use a command kubectl rollout

status and the deployment slash the deployment 
name. As we can see deployment rolling-demo

successfully rolled out. And if we describe the 
deployment using the kubectl describe command

kubectl describe deployment and the deployment 
name. And if we scroll up a little bit, so the

image name got updated to the 1.21 because we just 
rolled out with the newer version of the image. So

what's happening behind the scenes? Kubernetes 
uses max Unavailable to control how many pod can

be down during the update and maxSurge to allow 
creating extra pods temporarily. For example,

if you have three pods and max unavailable is one, 
it will update one pod at a time while keeping

at least two pods running. This makes the update 
smooth and undisruptive. What if the new version

has a bug? No worries. Kubernetes has your back. 
You can roll back to the previous working version

using the kubect rollout undo command. So, let's 
see it in the action as well. So, right now we

just updated it to the 1.21. But let's say we 
have some bugs in this particular version. So

we need to roll it back to the previous version 
that is 1.19. So this is the version which is our

previous working version. For that we can use a 
command kubectl rollout undo and the deployment

name deployment and the deployment name that is 
rolling-demo. So it got rolled back and that's

it. Kubernetes will roll you back to the previous 
stable version. So let's check it very quickly.

kubectl get pods pods in in the running state. And 
if we describe the deployment, we can see it got

updated to the 1.19 because we have we have rolled 
out it to the previous version. Now let's try this

out. Let's change the name to a faulty version. 
Let's say if we don't have any existing tag, we

will use it in the image. So for that we will use 
kubectl set image deploy and the deployment name

uh that is rolling-demo and I'm updating it to the 
image tag which does not exist. So it's broken.

Now let's check the status of the deployment. So 
it shows up and running pod it got failed because

if you can see it's not able to pull an image 
because that particular tag does not exist. But

if you see the older pod is working it's still 
in the running until and unless this particular

pod will comes in the running state this pod 
will not go away. And let's check the status of

the rollout kubectl roll out status deployment and 
the rolling hyphen demo. its demo. As you can see,

it's waiting for deployment to roll out to finish 
because if you notice our previous pod is in the

running state because our new pod we we just 
created, it's having some issues with the image

tag because that image tag does not exist. That's 
why it didn't deleted the previous pod. And now we

know it's a broken and it's not going to work. Now 
let's roll it back to the previous stable version.

For that we can use the same command kubectl roll 
out undo and the deployment and the deployment

name. It's rolling hyphen demo. It got rolled back 
to the previous working version. Let's do it very

quickly. As we can see, it's working fine. It just 
deleted the newer pod which we just created with

the broken tag. And if we describe the deployment 
and rolling demo, we can see it's working with the

1.19 tag itself. If you want to check the rollout 
history, so you can use a command kubectl rollout

history and the deploy / deployment name. So we 
can see the revisions of the application which

we did with the kubectl commands. This helps you 
track version and changes over the time as well.

Now let's understand when to use rolling updates 
and the roll backs. Use rolling updates when you

need zero downtime deployments. And if you want 
safe and gradual rollouts, you can use the rolling

updates over there. And if you need an easy way 
to roll back changes if something goes wrong,

just like we did for the broken tag, like 
the broken tag does not exist and it's not

able to pull an image. So our application got 
stuck because we are not able to create a pod.

So the older pod will remain up and running. 
But we need to roll it back to the previous up

working version. So in that case we need to use 
a roll backs. This is the perfect for production

environments especially when working in the CI/CD 
pipeline. So now you know how to perform rolling

updates and the roll backs in the Kubernetes. This 
is one of the key reasons why Kubernetes is loved

in the production grade deployments. We updated a 
live deployment, monitored it and rolled it back

safely all in a few commands. If this helped you, 
please don't forget to like, share, and subscribe

to the channel for more content like this. 
Thanks for watching. i will see you in next one.
